newsitem.title: UK: Japan's insurers face only slow change - industry.
newsitem.headline: Japan's insurers face only slow change - industry.

text.p: Agreement by Japan to open up its non-life insurance market will not lead to a rush of foreign competition, a leading European insurer told Reuters on Monday.

"It will allow efficient international companies to bring their experience of liberalised markets to Japan, but there won't be a massive increase in business. There won't be instant change," Royal & Sun Alliance international director Robin Rowland said.

Japan and the United States reached agreement on Saturday on how Japan should open its insurance industry to foreign competitors, a row that had grown into a major political issue between the two countries.

Rowland said the industry would have to see the precise details of the agreement before saying how much difference it would make, but he hoped it would create a level playing field for foreign insurers in Japan.
"My belief is that Japanese customers are no different to any others, They are perfectly able to choose between different types of products, although they will need some education."
"Japan was slipping behind the rest of the world in terms of freedom of choice for customers, both big and small," he added.

Royal & Sun Alliance has the largest presence of any European insurer in Japan, with projected premium income this year of around 80 million stg, said Rowland, who also chairs the Japan Committee of the British Invisibles trade organisation.
The Japanese insurance market is currently heavily regulated, with premium rates set in narrow bands by rating associations.
The new agreement should lead to deregulation, but Rowland said he expected that most Japanese would continue to buy their insurance from agents they felt happy with.
Foreign insurers currently have around three percent of the Japanese non-life market, which is the second largest in the world, and Rowland said he did not expect this figure to change very quickly.
He noted that some of the largest European insurance markets, including Germany and Italy, had only recently introduced greater pricing freedom.
